R03-C-01: It is tempting to treat superstition as a residue of ignorance, a set of mistaken beliefs that education will eventually wash away. The difficulty with this view is that superstition does not distribute itself the way ignorance does. Highly trained surgeons, pilots, stage actors and professional athletes, people who know a great deal about the causal workings of their craft, are often among the most attached to private rituals: a particular pair of socks, a fixed sequence of gestures before a performance, a refusal to say certain words aloud. If superstition were merely a gap in knowledge, these would be the last people we would expect to keep it. A more useful observation is that superstition gathers where two conditions meet: the outcome matters a great deal, and a significant part of it lies beyond the actor's control. Ethnographers have described fishing communities that use no protective magic when they work in a sheltered lagoon, where skill reliably brings a catch, yet surround voyages into the open sea with elaborate rites. The same people hold the same beliefs about the world; what changes is their exposure to chance. Examinations, sporting finals and opening nights share this structure. Preparation counts, but on the day itself something unaccountable remains, and the ritual fills the space that preparation cannot reach. What the ritual supplies, on this account, is not a causal lever over the outcome but a way of acting when no further useful action is available. Anxiety in the face of uncertainty tends to seek an outlet, and an outlet that is fixed, brief and familiar is better than one that is improvised, such as a last-minute change to a plan that was sound. A tennis player who bounces the ball exactly the same number of times before every serve is not, in any serious sense, trying to bend the laws of physics. She is marking a boundary between deliberation and execution, and the routine protects the execution from second thoughts. None of this makes superstition harmless. The same disposition that steadies a performer can lead a patient to choose a charm over a treatment that works, or a trader to mistake a lucky streak for a method. The line falls roughly where the ritual stops occupying the residue of chance and begins to displace action that would genuinely improve the odds. Understood this way, superstition is neither a quaint error to be laughed at nor a hidden wisdom to be celebrated, but a predictable human response to exposure that deserves to be judged by what it crowds out.
R03-C-02: A common modern objection to traditional mourning customs is that they put grief on a timetable. Many traditions mark fixed days after a death, often a gathering within the first two weeks, another around the fortieth day and a final observance at the first anniversary, and for centuries some communities prescribed the clothes a widow might wear and the months during which she should not appear at celebrations. To a sensibility that prizes authentic feeling, this looks like an intrusion: grief, it is said, is personal, it follows no calendar, and nobody has the right to tell a bereaved person when to stop. The objection contains a truth, but it misreads what the calendar was for. The fixed days rarely claimed to measure how long sorrow lasts. What they did was settle a set of practical questions that otherwise fall, at the worst possible moment, on the people least able to answer them. When should relatives visit, and when should they leave? What is it acceptable to say? When may the household resume ordinary work without seeming callous? A prescribed sequence answers all of these in advance, so that the bereaved are spared the labour of inventing their own conduct while they are exhausted, and so that neighbours know when their presence is expected. In this sense the timetable was addressed less to the mourner than to everyone around the mourner, translating an event that isolates one household into a sequence of obligations that the wider community could recognise and discharge. Its main work was coordination. Where such scripts have weakened, the result has not obviously been freer grief. Friends hesitate, unsure whether a call would comfort or intrude; colleagues say nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing; and the bereaved, told that they may grieve in their own way, often find that their own way is a lonely one, because nobody else knows what part to play in it. This is not an argument for restoring every old rule, nor for pretending that the old forms were uniformly benign. Some customs plainly bore down hardest on those with least power, and a widow who was obliged to wear mourning for years was being policed as much as consoled. The lesson is narrower. A society that abandons shared forms for mourning does not thereby hand grief back to the individual; it removes the cues that let others accompany it. Any replacement worth having would keep that coordinating function while dropping the demand that inner feeling match an outward schedule.
R03-C-03: Anthropologists have long described rites of passage as moving in three phases. The person undergoing the rite is first separated from an existing status, then passes through a transitional period in which he or she belongs to neither the old condition nor the new, and is finally incorporated into the community in a new role: adult, married, initiated, ordained. Of these phases the middle one, often called liminal, from the Latin word for a threshold, has attracted by far the most attention, and for good reason. It is there that most of the strange features of such rites are concentrated: seclusion in the forest or a special hut, the shaving of heads, the wearing of identical plain garments, the suspension of names, the imposition of hardship and silence. A simple reading treats these features as a waiting room, a pause while the real change, the conferral of new status, is prepared offstage. This misses their function. Stripping novices of names, clothing and possessions removes the markers by which they were previously ranked, so that for a time sons of important families and sons of poor ones are indistinguishable. Shared hardship then does two things at once. It makes the novices receptive to instruction, since people deprived of their usual footing listen differently, and it binds them to one another in a way that often outlasts the ritual, creating cohorts whose loyalty cuts across lineage and wealth. In recent decades, however, the idea has travelled far from its origins, and something has been lost on the way. The liminal phase is now often celebrated as a zone of freedom, creativity and play, and the word is applied to almost any in-between experience: the years after school, a period of unemployment, a long journey abroad. This enthusiasm overlooks how tightly the traditional threshold was managed. Elders set its length, prescribed what novices could eat and say, and decided when it was over. Its ambiguity was real, but it was ambiguity held inside a firm frame, and its whole point was the return. That frame is what most modern transitions lack. A young person who drifts between education and employment may experience the disorientation of the threshold without its discipline, its companions or, above all, its exit. There is no moment at which the community declares the passage complete and receives the person in a new capacity. None of this implies that the old rites should be revived, since their authority rested on forms of social life that no longer exist. But the comparison suggests that what made liminality productive was not the openness that its modern admirers praise. It was the certainty that the openness would end.
R03-C-04: There are two familiar ways of misunderstanding pilgrimage, and they are mirror images of each other. The first treats the journey as mere transport: what matters is arrival at the shrine, the sight of the image or the relic, the bath in the river, and the road is simply the price paid to get there. The second, popular among those who walk old pilgrim routes for reasons they would not call religious, reverses the emphasis. The destination, on this view, is almost a pretext; the real value lies in the walking itself, the days of effort, the strangers met on the way, the slow emptying of the mind. Each view captures something that pilgrims genuinely report, but both detach two elements that draw their meaning from each other, and neither can be made intelligible without the other. The hardships of the road are not valuable in the abstract. Blistered feet on a hiking holiday are an inconvenience; the same blisters on the way to a sacred place become an offering, a sign of seriousness, a story to be told on return. What converts them is the fixed point towards which they are directed. Equally, the shrine does not possess its full weight for the pilgrim independently of the effort spent reaching it. A visitor who arrives by car on a whim may see exactly what the pilgrim sees and still not have had the pilgrim's experience. The history of easier travel bears this interdependence out in an unexpected way, and it is worth dwelling on because it runs against a natural expectation. One might have predicted that when roads, railways and buses made distant shrines accessible within hours, the effortful element would simply vanish. In many places it has instead been reintroduced by choice. Pilgrims who have covered most of the distance in comfort often leave the vehicle to walk the final stretch, sometimes barefoot, sometimes on their knees. The effort has been condensed rather than abandoned, as though people sense that arrival without cost would not count as arrival at all. None of this means that the walker who sets out with no particular reverence is deceived about what he finds. Long days on foot do change people, and the change can be real without being religious. But it is worth noticing what such a walker relinquishes, perhaps without realising it, when the destination becomes optional rather than obligatory. The pilgrim cannot decide halfway that another town would do just as well, and that inability is part of what lends the road its gravity. A journey that could end anywhere is a fine thing; it is simply a different thing from one that must end in a particular place.
R03-C-05: Visitors to shrines that are frequented by people of more than one religion tend to come away with one of two stories. In the first, the shrine is evidence of a deep harmony beneath official differences: here, at the tomb of a holy figure or a spring credited with healing powers, ordinary believers ignore the boundaries their clergy insist on and share a common devotion. In the second, the arrangement is a fragile truce, a curiosity that survives only until politics catches up with it. Both stories are told about sites around the Mediterranean, in the Balkans and across South Asia, and both, I think, misdescribe what sharing usually involves. Close observation of such places rarely finds a single, blended faith. More often it finds parallel use. One community lights lamps in the evening, another comes on a particular weekday; one group knows the saint by one name and story, another by a different name and a different story, and neither is much troubled by the discrepancy. Custodians, frequently from one community, accept offerings from all and refrain from asking visitors what they believe. The sharing is real, but it consists in a set of practical accommodations rather than in agreement, and it works partly because certain questions are never posed: above all, the question of whose shrine it really is. This is why the harmony story, attractive as it is, puts the emphasis in the wrong place. The arrangement does not depend on people believing the same thing; it depends on their not being required to settle what they believe about this particular place. Nor does the truce story fare better. Many such sites have been shared for generations, through periods of considerable tension elsewhere, which is hard to square with the idea that their peace is merely a pause. What usually threatens them is not the slow pressure of difference but a sudden demand for definition, when some authority, a government department, a heritage body or a movement seeking to purify practice, insists that the site be registered, restored or claimed as belonging to one tradition alone. It would be romantic to pretend that these places were free of friction. Custodians could favour their own community, quarrels over offerings were common, and the vagueness that allowed sharing also allowed one side to quietly enlarge its claim. Still, the lesson they offer is more interesting than either of the usual stories. Coexistence, they suggest, need not wait for agreement about ultimate questions. It can rest on a carefully maintained ambiguity, which is a social achievement in its own right and, like most achievements, easier to destroy than to build.
R03-C-06: For much of the twentieth century, social scientists took it nearly for granted that modernisation and religion were locked in a zero-sum relationship. As societies industrialised, urbanised and educated their populations, faith would retreat, first from public life and then from private conviction. When the last decades of the century brought vigorous religious movements on several continents, and when religion returned to the centre of political argument in places where it had supposedly been tamed, many concluded that the secularisation thesis had simply been refuted. Some of its former defenders said as much. Both the confidence and the recantation, however, rested on treating as one hypothesis what was really a bundle of several. One strand concerns differentiation: the process by which law, medicine, education, science and the economy come to operate by their own criteria, no longer answerable to religious authority. A second concerns decline: a fall in belief, membership and practice among individuals. A third concerns privatisation: the withdrawal of religion from public argument into the domain of personal choice. These claims are logically independent. A society could see religious practice flourish while its hospitals, courts and universities remain entirely outside clerical control, and that combination is in fact common. Once the strands are separated, the evidence looks different. The decline thesis has fared poorly as a universal law; patterns of belief vary too widely between societies at similar levels of wealth to support it. The privatisation thesis has fared worse still, since religious voices are plainly present in public debate. But differentiation has held up remarkably well, and the point most often missed is that the religious resurgence itself tends to presuppose it. Movements that seek public influence organise as voluntary associations, compete for members, lobby legislatures, commission surveys and appeal to rights. They act, that is, as one set of claimants among many within institutions they do not control, which is precisely the condition that differentiation describes. It would be too quick to declare the older thesis vindicated by this route. A theory that predicted the fading of faith and got that prediction wrong in much of the world cannot be rescued by pointing to the part that survived, and some of its proponents did expect the strands to move together. The more modest conclusion is that the debate has been conducted at the wrong level of generality. To ask whether the world is becoming secular is to ask a question with no single answer; to ask which institutions have slipped free of religious authority, and on what terms religion now competes for influence within them, is to ask questions that the evidence can actually settle.
R03-C-07: Many societies have set aside days on which the ordinary order is turned upside down. In the Roman Saturnalia, masters are said to have waited on their slaves at table; in parts of medieval Europe, junior clergy elected a mock bishop and parodied the liturgy; in countless village festivals men dress as women, children give orders to adults, and the powerful are mocked in songs that would be punished at any other time of year. Such festivals of inversion have long puzzled those who study them, because they seem to put the most fundamental arrangements of a society at risk for the sake of a few days of licence. Two explanations have dominated. The first, often called the safety valve theory, holds that inversion protects the order it mocks. Resentments that accumulate under hierarchy are released in a bounded, harmless form, and when the festival ends everyone returns to their place, relieved and more willing to stay there. The second reverses the judgement. On this view, the festival gives people a glimpse of a world arranged otherwise, keeps alive the memory that rank is not natural, and so contains the seed of real defiance. Supporters of each view can point to cases. Rulers have tolerated and even funded such festivals, which suggests they found them useful; they have also banned them, which suggests they found them dangerous, and on a few occasions a carnival has indeed turned into a riot. What both explanations share is the assumption that the meaning of inversion is fixed by its form, so that one need only decide, once and for all, whether turning the world upside down conserves it or threatens it. The historical record does not support so tidy a choice, since the same festival, with the same masks and the same songs, has been a harmless frolic in one decade and the occasion of an uprising in the next. The difference lay not in the ritual but in its circumstances: a bad harvest, a disputed tax, a quarrel between factions of the elite that made the mockery of one of them useful to the other. Inversion, in other words, does not carry its own political charge; it takes one from the situation into which it is performed. The safety valve theory has a further weakness that is easy to overlook because its central image is so vivid. It pictures discontent as a kind of pressure that builds up in a closed vessel and can be let off in measured bursts. There is little reason to think that resentment, which is attached to particular injuries and particular persons, behaves like steam that can be vented without residue; people who have mocked their masters for a day do not obviously feel less aggrieved afterwards, and they may feel more entitled to their grievance for having heard it voiced aloud by a crowd. The image persuades because it is mechanical, not because anyone has observed the mechanism. A more promising account starts from a simpler observation. To turn a world upside down, one must first show which way up it is. The mock bishop presupposes a real one; the servant who gives orders for a day makes plain who gives them on every other day. Inversion is thus a vivid lesson in hierarchy, and in that sense it does teach the order it reverses. But the lesson cuts both ways, since a ranking that can be so easily reversed in play is shown to be a convention rather than a fact of nature. Which of these lessons is learned depends, again, on what else is happening. That is an unsatisfying conclusion only for those who wanted the festival to have a single meaning.
R03-C-08: Why do so many religious and quasi-religious groups ask their members to do things that are difficult, uncomfortable or expensive? Long fasts, pre-dawn prayers, restrictive diets, distinctive dress that invites ridicule, vows that forgo income or marriage: from a narrowly economic point of view these look like pure loss. An influential answer, borrowed from the study of animal behaviour, is that the costs are the point. A signal that is cheap to send can be sent by anyone, and so tells an observer little. A signal that is costly to send, and costlier still for someone who does not mean it, is credible precisely because it is hard to fake. Applied to ritual, the idea runs as follows. Groups that depend on mutual aid, sharing harvests, lending money or protecting one another, are vulnerable to people who take the benefits of membership without bearing its burdens. Demanding rituals screen such people out. Someone who is willing to rise before dawn for years, or to give up foods that everyone else enjoys, is unlikely to be only nominally attached, and the others can extend trust accordingly. The theory also explains a pattern that has often been remarked upon: groups that lower their demands in the hope of attracting members sometimes find that they lose them instead, as the value of belonging falls along with its cost. This is a genuinely illuminating account, and it captures something that purely symbolic interpretations of ritual tend to miss: that rituals are not only statements of meaning but also transactions with consequences for who can rely on whom, and that their cost is part of how they work rather than an unfortunate by-product. But it is incomplete in at least three ways. First, it explains why a ritual should be costly, not why it should take the particular form it does. Any sufficiently burdensome act would serve as a signal, yet communities care intensely about the precise words, gestures and times of their observances, and would not accept a different hardship of equal cost as a substitute. Second, many of the most demanding practices are imposed on children long before they could choose them. A rite performed on an infant may say something about the commitment of the parents, but it cannot be a signal of the child's own. The third gap is the most important. The signalling theory treats ritual as a message addressed to observers, as though the performer were already fully committed and merely needed to prove it. Yet people who undertake demanding practices commonly report that the practice changes them: that the fast or the vigil produces the conviction it was supposed to display. If that is so, cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it. A person who has sacrificed much for a group has reasons to value it that did not exist before the sacrifice, and the observer who reads his devotion as a signal is reading something that the ritual itself helped to create. None of these objections overturns the signalling account. They suggest instead that it describes one function among several, the one most visible to an outsider calculating whom to trust. A fuller theory would ask what ritual does to the people who perform it as well as what it tells the people who watch, and would treat the form of a rite as something that matters in its own right rather than as an arbitrary carrier of cost.
